turns.text:
I’d structure this as a 3-post research series, not one mega-post. The connective thesis is: **we keep talking about “agents” and “superintelligence,” but the real substrate is long-horizon reliability plus closed-loop improvement in the real world.**

**Post 1: Long-Running Task Systems**
Working title: **“The Agent Marathon: Why Long-Running Tasks Are Still Mostly Unsolved”**

Core thesis: The industry has moved from “can the model answer?” to “can an agent stay coherent across hours, tools, state, failures, and changing goals?” Current benchmarks show progress, but also expose that long-horizon autonomy is still brittle.

Outline:
1. **What counts as long-running?**
   - Not just long context.
   - Tasks with compounding state, partial observability, delayed reward, tool errors, and recovery.
   - Tie to METR’s “task-completion time horizon” framing: human-time duration at which agents succeed reliably.

2. **Benchmark landscape**
   - Software: SWE-Marathon, RALPHBench, SWE-EVO, RoadmapBench, LongCLI-Bench.
   - Terminal / ops: Terminal-Bench 2.0, LongCLI-Bench.
   - Web / open-world: Odysseys, WebArena lineage.
   - Business simulation: YC-Bench, Vending-Bench.
   - Memory: Agent Memory Benchmark.

3. **What the benchmarks agree on**
   - Models fail by losing state, over-parallelizing, misreading environment feedback, stopping early, or optimizing the wrong artifact.
   - Long-horizon success is less about one brilliant answer and more about repair loops.

4. **Open-source systems and tools**
   - OpenHands for software agents.
   - LangGraph / CrewAI / AutoGen / Microsoft Agent Framework / Pydantic AI / Mastra / Agno for orchestration.
   - OpenEvolve / CodeEvolve as algorithm-improvement agents.
   - Claude Code / Codex / OpenClaw style systems as practical long-session products.

5. **Industry state**
   - Frontier labs and coding products are pushing persistent sessions, skills, terminals, browser control, and issue-to-PR workflows.
   - But true “leave it alone for a day” reliability is still rare.

6. **Your angle**
   - “Long-running agents don’t need bigger prompts. They need black-box traces, resumable state, failure taxonomies, and proof protocols.”

Good source trail:
- METR time horizons: https://metr.org/time-horizons/
- RALPHBench: https://www.ralphbench.org/
- SWE-Marathon: https://swe-marathon.vercel.app/
- YC-Bench: https://collinear-ai.github.io/yc-bench/
- Odysseys: https://odysseys-website.pages.dev/
- LongCLI-Bench: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14337
- OpenHands paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16741
- AlphaEvolve: https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/

**Post 2: Self-Improvement**
Working title: **“Self-Improving AI Is Real, But Not the Way People Mean It”**

Core thesis: Public self-improvement is not recursive god-mode. It is a stack of increasingly strong loops: reflection, memory, prompt evolution, test-time correction, generated training data, evolutionary search, and production trace mining.

Outline:
1. **Define the ladder**
   - Level 0: retry / self-critique.
   - Level 1: reflection memory, e.g. Reflexion.
   - Level 2: skill libraries, e.g. Voyager.
   - Level 3: prompt/program optimization, e.g. GEPA, DSPy/MIPRO.
   - Level 4: test-time self-correction trained by RL, e.g. SCoRe.
   - Level 5: self-generated fine-tuning/update directives, e.g. SEAL.
   - Level 6: algorithm discovery loops, e.g. AlphaEvolve/OpenEvolve.
   - Level 7: lab-scale closed loops using proprietary traces, evals, synthetic data, and deployment feedback.

2. **What’s actually open**
   - Reflexion is old but still conceptually important.
   - GEPA is a strong public example of trace/reflection-driven prompt evolution.
   - SEAL is closer to weight-level adaptation, but still bounded research.
   - OpenEvolve shows the AlphaEvolve pattern is not conceptually secret, though frontier-scale execution may be.

3. **What frontier labs likely have that open source doesn’t**
   - Massive private trajectory corpora.
   - Reliable reward models / graders.
   - Production traces.
   - Secure sandboxes.
   - Human expert labels.
   - Compute for repeated rollouts.
   - Deployment feedback loops.

4. **Is self-improvement only frontier-lab magic?**
   - No for prompt/tool/system improvement.
   - Mostly yes for model-weight improvement at frontier scale.
   - The interesting middle ground is product teams that use traces → evals → prompt/runtime changes → held-out gates.

5. **Your angle**
   - “The self-improving system is not the model. It’s the harness.”

Good source trail:
- Reflexion: https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.11366
- GEPA: https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.19457
- SEAL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10943
- AlphaEvolve: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13131
- OpenEvolve: https://github.com/algorithmicsuperintelligence/openevolve
- SCoRe: https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12917
- Voyager: https://voyager.minedojo.org/

**Post 3: Superintelligence In The Wild**
Working title: **“If Superintelligence Arrives Quietly, What Would It Look Like First?”**

Core thesis: Superintelligence probably would not first look like a chatbot declaring itself. It would look like closed-loop systems that compress research, engineering, evaluation, and deployment cycles faster than institutions can observe.

Outline:
1. **Define the terms carefully**
   - OpenAI’s AGI definition: highly autonomous systems outperforming humans at most economically valuable work.
   - Bostrom-style superintelligence: greatly exceeding humans across virtually all domains of interest.
   - SSI’s public position: one goal, one product, safe superintelligence.

2. **Is superintelligence around us now?**
   - In the strong definition: no public evidence.
   - In narrow pockets: yes, we have superhuman systems in coding subproblems, protein/design/search/math fragments, retrieval, and optimization.
   - In organizational form: maybe the closest thing today is human+AI+eval+tooling loops compounding faster than competitors.

3. **The Ilya / SSI question**
   - SSI publicly says it has no product cycle distraction and is focused on safe superintelligence.
   - There is no public evidence that SSI has deployed “SSI” into live runs.
   - The responsible framing: “If SSI believes real-world interaction matters, what kind of non-public real-world loop would be consistent with its mission?”

4. **What “AI in the wild” could mean without a public product**
   - Internal research agents running experiments.
   - Closed sandboxes with real toolchains.
   - Synthetic companies / simulated labs / long-horizon environments.
   - Algorithm discovery loops.
   - Agent teams doing literature review, proof search, code optimization, red-teaming.
   - Private deployment to trusted researchers, not consumers.

5. **The real tell**
   - Not benchmark score.
   - Sustained autonomous research throughput.
   - Novel validated discoveries.
   - Ability to improve its own evals/tools safely.
   - Reliable transfer from sandbox to messy reality.

6. **Your angle**
   - “Superintelligence may first appear as an operating cadence, not a product.”

Good source trail:
- SSI official: https://ssi.inc/
- Axios on SSI funding / no product plan: https://www.axios.com/2024/09/05/ilya-sutskevers-ai-startup-raise
- OpenAI Charter AGI definition: https://openai.com/charter/
- Bostrom definition: https://nickbostrom.com/superintelligence
- Dwarkesh/Ilya episode summary: https://www.tapesearch.com/episode/dwarkesh-and-ilya-sutskever-on-what-comes-after-scaling/9H4vn7L2gPKLaenJWdWnM4
- Anthropic RSP / frontier safety framing: https://www.anthropic.com/news/responsible-scaling-policy-v3

**Best Series Framing**
Title: **“The Long Horizon”**

Subtitle: **Agents, self-improvement, and the quiet path to superintelligence.**

The throughline:
1. Long-running tasks are the empirical bottleneck.
2. Self-improvement is the mechanism for crossing it.
3. Superintelligence, if it arrives, may look first like a closed-loop institution that learns faster than humans can audit.
